ety.text: From Middle English alas, from Old French a las (French hélas), from a (“ah”) + las, from Latin lassus (“weary”). Compare Dutch helaas, North Frisian ielas, West Frisian eilaas.

senses.d: Used to express sorrow, regret, compassion, grief, resignation, or disappointment.
ex: I wanted to catch the last bus home, but alas, I was ten minutes late and had to take a taxi instead.

Helas I lamente the dull abuſyd brayne
The enfatuate fantaſies the wytles wylfulnes
Of on and hothyr at me that haue dyſdayne

senses.d: A type of geological depression formed by the subsidence of permafrost, sometimes (partially) filled by a lake.

fr:hélas.gl: alas; exclamatory or declarative conjunction expressing affliction, regret, disappointme…

ety.text: Inherited from Old French elas, variant of a las, from a (“ah”) + las, from Latin lassus (“weary”).

pt:ai de mim.gl: alas, woe is me (exclamation of sorrow)

ety.text: From Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹 (wai, “woe”), from Proto-Germanic *wai, both from Proto-Indo-European *wai.
From Middle English alarme, alarom, borrowed from Middle French alarme, itself from Old Italian all'arme! (“to arms!, to the weapons!”), ultimately from Latin arma (“arms, weapons”).

senses.d: A summons to arms, as on the approach of an enemy.
ex: Arming to answer in a night alarm.

senses.d: Any sound or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a warning sound to arouse attention; a warning of danger.
ex: Sound an alarm in my holy mountain.

senses.d: A device intended to warn or give notice of approaching danger.
ex: The fire alarm is located high on the wall to prevent tampering.

Lord Marshal, command our officers-at-arms
Be ready to direct these home alarms.

Is it then true, as distant rumours run,
that crowds of rivals for thy mother's charms
thy Palace fill with insults and alarms?

senses.d: Sudden surprise with fear or terror caused by the apprehension of danger; a feeling of heightened alertness to risk.
ex: His actions caused alarm among all the other people in the store, who hurried to leave.
Alarm and resentment spread through the camp.

senses.d: A mechanical device for awaking people or rousing their attention.
ex: The clock radio is a friendlier version of the cold alarm by the bedside.

senses.d: An instance of an alarm ringing, beeping or clanging, to give a noise signal at a certain time.
ex: Last night's alarm turned out to be nothing, but it was terrifying at the time.

senses.d: To call to arms for defense.
To give (someone) notice of approaching danger or necessary action; to rouse to vigilance; to put on the alert.
ex: The sudden drop in temperature should alarm you into taking precautions.
Her illness started to alarm the doctors, who ordered more tests.

senses.d: To produce a warning of approaching danger or necessary action; to emit a signal intended to rouse a recipient to vigilance or put them on the alert.
To surprise with apprehension of danger; to fill with anxiety in regard to threatening evil; to excite with sudden fear.
ex: The loud bang in the hallway seemed to alarm everyone in the building.

senses.d: To keep in excitement; to disturb.

grp.label: sudden surprise with fear or terror
instance of an alarm ringing or clanging
to give notice (by sound or otherwise) of approaching danger

ety.text: Borrowed from Italian all'arme (“to arms”), with univerbation. Compare alerte.
Univerbation of all' (“to the”) + arme (“weapons”, archaic plural of arma), literally “to the weapons, to arms”.
Borrowed from Italian all'arme, allarme; see also French alarme.
Arabic رَابَطَ (rābaṭa)der. Arabic رِبَاط (ribāṭ) Andalusian Arabic رباط (ribāt)bor. Spanish rebato Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic رباط (ribāt).
Borrowed from French alarme, from Italian all'arme (“to arms”).
From alarme + -ar or from French alarmer.

ex: I'm extremely alarmed about the army outside my house.
Thomas, the groom, in the act of drinking, put down the jug alarmed before his master. Thomas’s master felt the honour keenly.

senses.d: Causing apprehension, fear or alarm; frightening.
